entities.name: Bath Abbey
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
Bath Abbey (Abbey Church of Saint Peter and Saint Paul, Bath) is a magnificent Perpendicular Gothic church in Bath, England, built primarily between 1499 and 1616 CE. Located at the heart of one of England's most historic cities — a Roman spa city reactivated by Georgian tourism — the Abbey is famous for its dramatic fan vaulting, its unusual 'Jacob's ladder' west façade featuring angels climbing and descending to heaven, and its status as the site of England's first recorded coronation.

Bath Abbey was founded as a Benedictine monastery in the 7th century. The Norman cathedral that preceded the current building was the scene of Edgar's coronation in 973 CE — the first coronation of all England, establishing a ceremony template used to this day. The current building was begun by Bishop Oliver King in 1499, who reportedly dreamed of angels ascending and descending ladders between heaven and earth — inspiring the distinctive tower carvings. Construction halted during the Dissolution of the Monasteries (1539) leaving the roof unfinished for 75 years.

Elizabeth I intervened to have Bath Abbey reroofed after visiting in 1574, observing the building exposed to rain. Queen Victoria funded restoration in the 1860s. The Abbey's Perpendicular Gothic interior creates a 'lantern church' effect — nearly half the wall area is glass from 52 windows. Famous residents interred include the mathematician James Montagu and explorer James Quin, while a famous wall tablet commemorates Beau Nash, Bath's Georgian social arbiter.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Bath Abbey hosted England's first unified coronation in 973 CE, establishing a ceremony template used for every subsequent British monarch, making it foundational to British monarchical tradition despite its modest size.
